title: Depressurizing Our Relationships: The Day Mr. Rogers Stopped Judging
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: This interlude in Dave Stuart Jr.'s series on depressurizing the teacher soul looks at the social side of burnout through the story of Fred Rogers as a seminary student. Rogers sat in judgment of a poor sermon until he saw that the friend beside him was moved to tears by it, and he learned that she had come in need while he had come in judgment. Stuart argues that releasing judgment is not a moral rule but a recognition of reality: our perspective is only a sliver, and judging others is an inner whirlpool that isolates us. He admits he once enjoyed maligning weak colleagues and calls that inclusion by exclusion. He concludes that a person's value does not come from performance, and he shows how the intellect, body and emotions can habituate non-judgment while feedback stays businesslike rather than personal.
points: The Fred Rogers story shows that the difference between two listeners lay in the posture each brought, need versus judgment.
Judgment is presented as irrational rather than merely impolite, because one person's view of reality is too narrow to be definitive.
Gossip about weak colleagues feels safe and inclusive but rests on the mistaken idea that people are their performance.
Letting go of judgment relieves pressure, and teachers can still give necessary feedback by keeping it about the work, not the person.
quotes: The social aspect of us is special because it’s the part of us that’s not just us.

Fred’s perception of reality was just a sliver; so why go on pretending that his sliver was the definitive one? What was the value in sitting there during a sermon, miserably cataloguing mistakes, when the person next to him was getting a heart message, was deepening spiritually?

But the speaker wasn’t proposing a rule to follow any more than Newton was with gravity. He was indicating a law — a fundamental reality. He was saying, “Listen: you don’t know it all. You’re not that big. Judging is an inner whirlpool. You’ll end up drowned, separated, and lonely. It’ll bring you down.
I’ll say it — it felt good to judge. It felt safe. It was inclusion by exclusion.

But driving home one day, I had a realization: a person’s value doesn’t come from their performance. Because we’re not our jobs. We’re not our actions. We’re not our competencies. We’re people. People are more than performance.

When Fred Rogers committed himself against judging, he opened up a permanent depressurization valve on his soul. He didn’t need to measure himself against other people; he didn’t need to worry if other people measured him. He just needed to show up, do his best, and trust forces beyond himself to fill in any gaps — just like they did for his friend during the sermon.
2) You and I do have to give feedback sometimes, but it never has to be a personal judgment. It can be business.
